captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 8. In this lesson: Screen time.
Read an article that uses expert opinion and statistics.
Here are some new words. Screen time. The time someone spends looking at a phone, computer or ti vi.
Wellbeing. Being healthy, comfortable and happy. Addictive. Making you want to do something again and again.
And some more words. Notification. A message or alert on a phone. Algorithm.
A set of rules a computer follows, for example to choose what you see. Moderation.
Not doing too much of something.
Time for a question. The video will stop.
Which word means: the time someone spends looking at a phone, computer or ti vi?
Now some grammar: Quantifiers with statistics.
Use quantifiers to describe numbers in a text: the majority of, a minority of, nearly half, over a third,
very few. For example: The majority of teenagers own a phone. For example: Nearly half said they slept badly.
Now listen, and read along. Is screen time really so bad?
Teenagers today spend an average of seven hours a day looking at screens outside school.
But is this a problem? According to a recent survey of 2,000 students aged 12 to 15,
the majority use their phones to talk to friends, and over a third use them for homework. However,
nearly half said they often stayed up late because of their phones,
and a quarter felt anxious when they couldn't check their notifications. Dr Lena Hart,
a psychologist who studies digital wellbeing, believes the type of screen time matters more than the amount.
‘Video-calling your grandmother or learning to code is very different from scrolling for hours,’ she explains.
‘Many apps use algorithms designed to keep you watching. That can be addictive.’
Her advice? ‘Use technology in moderation.
Turn off notifications at night, and keep your phone out of your bedroom.’
Another question. The video will stop. How long do teenagers spend on screens outside school on average?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like screen time, wellbeing, addictive.
You practised quantifiers with statistics. And you read Is screen time really so bad?
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 8. In this lesson: If I had known.
Use the third conditional to talk about past regrets and imagined results.
Here are some new words. Regret. Feel sorry about something you did or didn't do. Privacy.
The right to keep personal information to yourself. Password. A secret word that lets you into an account.
And some more words. Scam. A dishonest trick to get money or information. Suspicious.
Making you think something is wrong. Report. Tell someone in authority about a problem.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: feel sorry about something you did or didn't do?
Now some grammar: Third conditional.
Use If plus past perfect, would have plus past participle to imagine a different past.
For example: If I had checked the link, I wouldn't have lost my account.
For example: She would have reported it if she had known.
Now listen, and read along. Sam's story: a lesson learned.
Last year I got a message that looked like it came from my favourite on lai game.
It said I had won 5,000 free coins and just needed to ‘confirm my account’.
I was so excited that I clicked the link and typed in my username and password.
The next morning, I couldn't log in. Someone had changed my password and taken all my items.
Looking back, the message was suspicious.
The spelling was strange, and the link didn't go to the real website.
If I had checked the link more carefully, I wouldn't have lost my account.
If I had used two-step verification, the scammer couldn't have got in, even with my password.
I reported the scam to the game company, and they helped me recover some things.
Now I never click links in messages that offer prizes – and I tell my friends to do the same.
Another question. The video will stop. What did the message promise?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like regret, privacy, password. You practised third conditional.
And you read Sam's story: a lesson learned. Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

A.prompt: Read “Is screen time really so bad?”. True or false?  “Nearly half of the students often stayed up late because of their phones.”
A.ctx:
Is screen time really so bad?
Teenagers today spend an average of seven hours a day looking at screens outside school. But is this a problem?
According to a recent survey of 2,000 students aged 12–15, the majority use their phones to talk to friends, and over a third use them for homework. However, nearly half said they often stayed up late because of their phones, and a quarter felt anxious when they couldn't check their notifications.
Dr Lena Hart, a psychologist who studies digital wellbeing, believes the type of screen time matters more than the amount. ‘Video-calling your grandmother or learning to code is very different from scrolling for hours,’ she explains. ‘Many apps use algorithms designed to keep you watching. That can be addictive.’
Her advice? ‘Use technology in moderation. Turn off notifications at night, and keep your phone out of your bedroom.’
